item.title: Tesla opens 14 Semi Megacharger stalls between Atlanta and Savannah
item.description:
Tesla has opened its first Semi Megacharger sites in the Southeast: an 8-stall station just south of Atlanta and a 6-stall station outside Savannah, each rated for up to 1.2 MW per stall.

The Savannah site is also the first Megacharger at a Pilot truck stop, a rollout that was supposed to start this summer. Together, the two stations give the Tesla Semi its first public charging corridor outside California.

item.title: Trump's crackdown on foreign students and workers
item.description:
The Trump administration announced yesterday that it will no longer allow Microsoft, Adobe, and a handful of other companies to sponsor foreign workers for green cards and accused nine universities of abusing the J-1 temporary student visa program. Earlier this week, it also proposed a rule raising the fee for international students who want to stay in the U.S. and work temporarily through the Optional Practical Training program from about $500 to $70,000. We have more. Then, will Minnesotan restaurants be willing to dish up invasive crayfish?

item.title: Attorney urges care in choosing Secretary of State
item.description:
Having practiced law for over 45 years, I can confirm that the Secretary of State is an office way too critical to be a political football. It’s a shame the election is even a partisan one.

The SOS protects the right to vote for every eligible voter and works with local officials to provide efficient, transparent, and fair elections. Thanks to state and local professionals and local volunteers, elections have never been a problem here. The SOS also handles campaign finance reports, registers lobbyists, processes ballot questions, commissions notaries, and delivers a host of other services to individuals and local governments.

The SD SOS also is critical to businesses and consumers in this state. SOS maintains information for all business entities operating in South Dakota and makes that information available online.

The office handles over 70,000 business filings each year, plus trademarks and Uniform Commercial Code filings important to lenders and property owners.

Dedication to competent, efficient, professional service is crucial.

Knowing all that, Republican incumbent Monae Johnson endorsed Terrence Davis. Despite the personal costs of endorsing a Democrat, Johnson explained that she could not remain silent because “the integrity, stability, and professionalism of this office is at stake.”

Likely, that’s because Republican candidate Heather Baxter is known as an election denier who neither respects the strength of our existing system nor understands the broad duties of the SOS.

Baxter ran for SOS only after coming in last in a primary election earlier this year for a legislative seat in her home district. Her focus is what she calls “election reform” – a euphemism for abandoning automation in favor of an inefficient, error-riddled plan of hand-counting all ballots.

Davis is a competent, reality-based professional who knows election administration is only one part of the job and knows it should not be politicized.

A former SD state trooper, Davis has a Master’s in public policy and experience in law enforcement and legal services, and is working on a doctorate in Law and Policy.

He respects the expertise of County Auditors, is committed to protecting voter information, and supports careful testing before implementing any major changes. Instead of retreating to pre-automation days, he advocates modernizing website services for businesses and consumers alike.

Terrence Davis, as Monae Johnson knows, is the best choice for SD Secretary of State.

Nancy Turbak Berry has practiced law in Watertown for 42 years. She has been a state senator, a state court magistrate judge, and an adjunct law professor.

Photo: Terrence Davis

item.title: Don't move a muscle!
item.description:
First-time unemployment claims (layoffs, basically) have come in below 200,000 for four weeks running — the longest stretch since 1969. At the same time, the economy only barely added jobs in September. Few layoffs, barely any new jobs, and it makes ya start to wonder, just how petrified can this labor market get? Also in this episode: AI doomers touch grass at a monthly Bay Area picnic, the personal savings rate ebbs to a 4-year low, and Kai explains central bankers’ balance sheet agita.

item.title: How a Meta AI prompt changed one mom’s approach to online privacy
item.description:
It started when Kalie Robins posted an Instagram video with her kid. Meta's built in AI chatbot, Muse, started prompting her to ask questions about her daughters and personal life, which sent her down a social-media-privacy rabbit hole.


Robins took to her feed — at the time, with only a few hundred followers — to share her experience. “It starts pulling completely separate information for each of my kids: their names, birth information, pictures and videos of them. And then it says, ‘pinpointing Kalie Robbins' location,’” she said in her now viral video.


Meta responded to the incident saying it “missed the mark” and has fixed the issue that prompted those questions.


But Robins says she's now been catapulted into the AI privacy discourse. And it's pretty uncomfortable.


More on this:


Mother Horrified When Meta’s AI Scours Instagram and Facebook for Invasive Information About Her Young Daughters — from Futurism

item.title: Why is Trump gutting a rural renewable energy program?
item.description:
The USDA just issued a final ruling that will effectively end federal support for renewable energy projects on cropland. The program is The Rural Energy for America Program (REAP). 

The decision is in keeping with President Trump’s long-standing hostility toward wind- and solar-energy projects. With regard to projects supported by REAP, the Trump administration, through Agriculture Secretary Brooke R. Rollins, calls them “unreliable” and adds that they “have not fully delivered on their stated goals.” 

As to federal support,  Rollins says, “as of today that ends.”

South Dakota has participated in the program, to the tune of millions of dollars, in scattered parts of the state. USDA has touted the success of its projects in South Dakota, one of numerous states that have seen similar REAP-funded success stories.  

Given that backdrop, the USDA decision to drop the program seems arbitrary and contrary to its history of success.

Indeed, EARTHJUSTICE, which describes itself as the nation’s “premier nonprofit public interest environmental law organization,” has filed a lawsuit against USDA, challenging its gutting of REAP.

Says EARTHJUSTICE: “For decades, REAP had been a smashing success story. Since 2014, 19,000 farms and rural small businesses across all 50 states received REAP awards from USDA. According to USDA, in 2024 alone, the program awarded over $1 billion in REAP grants and loan guarantees nationwide, and generated or saved enough energy to power more than 300,000 homes. As late as May 2025, USDA touted REAP success stories, including the purchase of a 1.5 MW solar array by a farm in Habersham County, Georgia, which would “realize $176,490 per year of income and will generate 2,206 MWh per year, enough to power 204 homes.” 

My take? I want to see some specificity from USDA as to how many REAP projects have been “unreliable” and “have not delivered as promised.” USDA itself boasts about the history of the program. Success stories in South Dakota and other states have had uniformly positive outcomes.

We need endeavors like REAP. Climate change is a fact. Says NASA, “there is unequivocal evidence that Earth is warming at an unprecedented rate. Human activity is the principal cause.”

Seems logical that the USDA should do all it can to facilitate the downshift of a man-made process that could do all of us in if we don’t change our ways.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.

item.source:markdown:
The USDA [just issued a final ruling](https://whig.com/2026/10/06/usda-rule-discourages-solar-and-wind-projects-on-cropland/) that will effectively end federal support for renewable energy projects on cropland. The program is The Rural Energy for America Program (REAP).
The decision is in keeping with President Trump’s [long-standing hostility](https://www.eenews.net/articles/what-clean-energy-bosses-say-about-trumps-attacks-on-renewables-2/) toward wind- and solar-energy projects. With regard to projects supported by REAP, the [Trump administration](https://wtaq.com/2026/10/05/usda-issues-final-rule-with-comment-period-ahead-of-opening-the-application-window-for-rural-energy-for-america-program/), through Agriculture Secretary Brooke R. Rollins, calls them “unreliable” and adds that they “have not fully delivered on their stated goals.”
As to federal support, Rollins says, “as of today that ends.”
South Dakota has [participated in the program](https://mitchellnow.com/news/236632-usda-rural-development-investments-in-south-dakota/), to the tune of [millions of dollars](https://www.cfra.org/blog/rural-energy-program-benefits-south-dakota-businesses), in [scattered parts](https://drgnews.com/2024/10/24/south-dakota-businesses-receive-more-than-1-8-million/) of the state. USDA has [touted the success](https://www.rd.usda.gov/files/success-story/SD-REAPProgram.pdf#:~:text=In%20South%20Dakota%2C%20some%20of,grain%20dryers%2C%20LED%20lighng%2C%20coolers%2C) of its projects in South Dakota, one of numerous states that have seen similar [REAP-funded success stories](https://elpc.org/resources/reap-success-stories/).
Given that backdrop, the USDA decision to drop the program seems arbitrary and contrary to its history of success.
Indeed, [EARTHJUSTICE](https://earthjustice.org/about), which describes itself as the nation’s “premier nonprofit public interest environmental law organization,” has [filed a lawsuit](https://earthjustice.org/experts/michael-youhana/the-trump-administration-says-it-wants-to-help-farmers-so-why-is-it-taking-solar-away-from-them) against USDA, challenging its gutting of REAP.
Says EARTHJUSTICE: “ _For decades, REAP had been a smashing success story. Since 2014, 19,000 farms and rural small businesses across all 50 states received REAP awards from USDA. According to USDA, in 2024 alone, the program awarded over_ [_$1 billion in REAP grants and loan guarantees nationwide_](https://www.rd.usda.gov/rural-data-gateway/rural-investments/program-areas) _, and generated or saved_ [_enough energy to power more than 300,000 homes_](https://www.usda.gov/sites/default/files/documents/32-2026-CJ-RBCS.pdf) _. As late as May 2025, USDA touted_ [_REAP success stories_](https://www.usda.gov/sites/default/files/documents/32-2026-CJ-RBCS.pdf) _, including the purchase of a 1.5 MW solar array by a farm in Habersham County, Georgia, which would “realize $176,490 per year of income and will generate 2,206 MWh per year, enough to power 204 homes.”_
My take? I want to see some specificity from USDA as to how many REAP projects have been “unreliable” and “have not delivered as promised.” USDA itself [boasts](https://www.rd.usda.gov/files/success-story/SD-REAPProgram.pdf#:~:text=In%20South%20Dakota%2C%20some%20of,grain%20dryers%2C%20LED%20lighng%2C%20coolers%2C) about the history of the program. Success stories in South Dakota and other states have had uniformly positive outcomes.
We need endeavors like REAP. Climate change is a fact. [Says NASA](https://science.nasa.gov/climate-change/), “there is unequivocal evidence that Earth is warming at an unprecedented rate. Human activity is the principal cause.”
Seems logical that the USDA should do all it can to facilitate the downshift of a man-made process that could do all of us in if we don’t change our ways.
_John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission._

item.title: Trump tariffs are a work in progress … except there’s been no progress
item.description:
Here’s yesterday’s headline from CNBC: “U.S. trade deficit hits $106.billion, widest since just before Trump tariffs enacted last year.”

That deflating news comes as no surprise.

Along with a ton of other people who have even a particle of knowledge on the subject, I’ve been pounding on Trump’s tariff policy since his first term. Basically, we skeptics argued that the president's tariff plan is bad for the economy and won’t do much good for our balance of trade.

Well, much as I hate to say ‘I told you so’ … I told you so.

August’s balance of trade numbers just came out, and at $106.5 billion, it's the widest gap since that jingoistic “liberation day” speech on April 2, 2025, which he said was “a date that  will forever be remembered as the day American industry was reborn, the day America's destiny was reclaimed, and the day that we began to Make America Wealthy Again." 

Trump then held up a chart, later widely ridiculed, which he claimed was proof that “foreign leaders have stolen our jobs,  foreign cheaters have ransacked our factories, and foreign scavengers have torn apart  our once beautiful American dream.”

Looking for Trump-friendly support somewhere, anywhere, I find that supporters of the president’s trade policies are concentrated in a strongly conservative wing of the Republican party. Outside of that circle I can’t find much in the way of agreement with Trump, particularly among experts in the field.

Fact is, there isn’t much in the way of results that indicate Trump’s tariffs have done any good.

As to Trump’s rhetoric on “liberation day,” it  was not only head-shakingly hyperbolic, it was all wrong. 

Trump’s tariffs have hurt, not helped, the American economy. AI sums it up: “These import taxes function as a direct financial burden that U.S. companies and families ultimately pay.” 

Despite August’s leap to the upside, the overall 2026 trade deficit is lower than last year (by 20%) – an outcome which is to be expected after Trump’s tariff frenzy. As to positive gains for the economy,  mmm, the reduction has yet to bear any fruit. So far this year GDP growth is loping along at around 2%, about unchanged from 2025. As to inflation, this year’s rate of 3.37% is considerably higher than 2025’s 2.68%. 

Researchers at the Federal Reserve Board last spring found that Trump’s tariffs have contributed nearly a percentage point to inflation, an outcome that was widely predicted by mainstream economists, including 16 Nobel laureates.

Trump ignored ample counsel and proceeded to turn his half-baked tariff scheme into a fully-baked tariff scam.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.

item.title: AI spending takes center stage ahead of midterms

item.title: What a less dominant America might mean for your money
item.description:
I have long suggested owning companies outside the United States as part of a diversified investment portfolio. For most of that time it was unpopular advice. Americans did well betting on America, and the habit of holding primarily US stocks is deeply entrenched. Our brains are emotionally wired to buy what is familiar and hold what has increased in value.

American investors keep about 81% of their stock holdings at home, according to research from Vanguard, even though American companies make up roughly 60% of the world's stock markets.

A reason to look at that gap comes in a report by Phillips Payson O'Brien, titled "The American Age Is Over," published September 16, 2026, in The Atlantic. O'Brien, a professor of strategic studies at the University of St Andrews in Scotland, writes: "The American age that followed World War II was bound to end eventually. What's shocking is how suddenly that moment has arrived."

O'Brien builds part of his case on this year's war with Iran. In addition to the immediate costs of the war, stockpiles of the most advanced American munitions will take years to rebuild.

He also points out that longtime American partners are making their own arrangements, with Pakistan, Turkey, and Saudi Arabia signing a defense pact and South Korea warming to China. O'Brien sees this as part of a slower change that was already underway, writing, "The emergence of East Asia as the center of the world's economic output was always going to reduce American influence."

Both of these factors may affect your money. For example, China makes about 50% of the world's ships and controls about 80% of its drone manufacturing. The second and third largest shipbuilders are Japan and South Korea, while the United States does almost no civilian shipbuilding.

The other side of the case comes in a September 2, 2026, column in Directors & Boards, titled "The Shining City on a Hill," by Robert H. Rock. Rock grants that America has lost standing abroad, then writes: "Paradoxically, America's reputation abroad has weakened at the same time America's relative economic advantages have strengthened."

Only time will tell whether either O’Brien or Rock is right. In the meantime, it would not be helpful to overreact to either prediction. Neither fear nor unthinking confidence has much to do with the evidence.  

What evidence does show is that a portfolio concentrated in one country does well only when that country does well into the future. The same thing is true of a nation's currency. If you earn dollars, spend dollars, and hold only dollar assets, you have taken a huge bet on the dollar, whether you intended to or not.

Let me emphasize that I am NOT suggesting the United States is finished or that you sell your American holdings. What I do suggest is that it would be worthwhile to consider what a less dominant America might mean for your money. Here are some suggestions: If you own index or target date funds, look at what is inside of them, because many hold American equities first, then international. Any additional  money you add could be diversified into international companies that earn in yen, euros, and pounds. If you are close to retirement, consider holding three years of living expenses in reserves to protect against needing to sell at the bottom of a market. Above all, make any changes gradually.

Diversifying your portfolio across the globe will not completely insulate you from a bad year in equities, because global markets tend to rise and fall together. However, that diversification can help shield your retirement resources from the decline of any single country.

item.title: What could slowing the AI frontier mean for the economy?
item.description:
The AI industry appears to be getting more serious about safety.


Leaders of top companies signed a non-binding agreement at the White House Sept. 30, laying out standards and best practices for responsible development of advanced AI. OpenAI delayed the release of its latest model due to safety concerns. And Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called on the sector to slow things down and "pace the frontier."


Wall Street initially wasn't too happy about that push and stocks related to the AI buildout took a momentary tumble.


But Jordan Nanos, at the chip research and consulting firm SemiAnalysis, argues that greater investment in AI security could actually drive more demand for computing power.
item.source:markdown:
The AI industry appears to be getting more serious about safety.
Leaders of top companies signed a non-binding [agreement](https://d3i6fh83elv35t.cloudfront.net/static/2026/09/accord.pdf) at the White House Sept. 30, laying out standards and best practices for responsible development of advanced AI. OpenAI [delayed the release of its latest model due to safety concerns](https://www.wsj.com/tech/ai/openai-chatgpt-model-release-cancel-safety-5a2f9f42). And Anthropic CEO [Dario Amodei](https://darioamodei.com/post/we-must-pace-the-frontier) called on the sector to slow things down and "pace the frontier."
[Wall Street initially wasn't too happy about that push](https://www.businessinsider.com/stock-market-slow-down-ai-development-dario-amodei-ai-trade-2026-9) and stocks related to the AI buildout took a momentary tumble.
But Jordan Nanos, at the chip research and consulting firm SemiAnalysis, argues that greater investment in AI security could actually drive _more_ demand for computing power.

item.title: Lucid (LCID) Q3 deliveries drop 7% as it slashes production by 38%
item.description:
Lucid (LCID) delivered 3,806 vehicles in the third quarter, down 7% from a year ago. It built only 2,954, a 38% cut from the previous quarter and its lowest production since early 2025.

The automaker says that’s on purpose. New CEO Silvio Napoli is selling down the unsold cars Lucid piled up in the first half of the year, and Q3 is the first quarter of 2026 in which it delivered more vehicles than it built.

more…

item.title: Rounds' gas tax holiday? It's pandering. It's a terrible idea
item.description:
Our Sen. Rounds just wrote a letter to the White House urging President Trump to suspend federal gasoline and diesel taxes through the end of the year. If you read the letter, you’ll see that Rounds is blaming a multitude of geo-political events, armed conflicts included, for the shortage of fuel that’s costing all of us plenty.

Rounds, like every other Republican running for office, is confronting an election season that sees GOP leader Trump in serious trouble with the electorate.The president’s approval ratings are dismal, so it comes as no surprise that Republican candidates are working overtime to find popular initiatives to curry some favor with voters. Rounds’ ploy is just another one of those rabbits coming out of a hat that is probably running low on schemes to bolster public support for the GOP. 

This one is particularly obnoxious because its consequences are insidious and long term in nature. It sounds like a great, populist idea, just perfect for mesmerizing voters with its promise of cheaper fuel, but a gas  tax holiday has costs that will result in serious longer term problems.

And not only that, it really doesn’t save you all that much money.

  • First off, as that doyenne of conservative thought, the Cato Institute, puts it, a gas tax holiday would be “expensive, ineffective and fiscally irresponsible.” Says Cato: “A three-month gas tax holiday would either accelerate the Highway Trust Fund’s insolvency by roughly nine months or require at least an $11 billion general-fund bailout. Meanwhile, the average driver would save only about $3 per fill-up.”

  • The Tax Policy Center, calling a federal gas tax holiday a “terrible idea,” makes the economic argument that a holiday would “increase consumption at a time of low supply, thus driving up pre-tax prices and worsening climate change.”

  • The Budget Lab calculates that a 3-month federal gas tax holiday would save the average household roughly $37. Whoopee.

  • The Tax Foundation headlines “Gas Tax Holidays Sound Politically Tempting. Too Bad They Don’t Work.” The Tax Foundation calls attention to the fact that “pausing fuel taxes makes funding roads and highways more difficult while doing nothing to address the underlying issues driving prices upward.”

It’s tough to find supportive economic arguments for a gas tax holiday. In fact, I found it impossible. AI can steer you to a lot of verbiage about how it makes the government look like it’s doing something to help already cash-strained consumers. Trouble is, the argument overlooks the fact that the government’s economic and trade policies are responsible for making financial life tough for consumers in the first place. 

Rounds won’t let up on his facile support for a gas tax holiday and of course will never acknowledge that people are financially strained because his party’s economic policies were fatally flawed from the get-go.

Will all this tax holiday talk do Republicans much good in November? I doubt it. The party’s rhetoric on inflation is transparently hopeless. Promoting a scheme like a gas tax holiday is another helping of GOP malarkey on the subject.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.

item.source:markdown:
Our Sen. Rounds just [wrote a letter](https://www.rounds.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/senator_rounds_letter_on_dpa_and_gas_tax.pdf) to the White House urging President Trump to suspend federal gasoline and diesel taxes through the end of the year. If you read the letter, you’ll see that Rounds is blaming a multitude of geo-political events, armed conflicts included, for the shortage of fuel that’s costing all of us plenty.
Rounds, like every other Republican running for office, is confronting an election season that sees GOP leader Trump in serious trouble with the electorate.The president’s approval ratings [are dismal](https://www.natesilver.net/p/trump-approval-ratings-nate-silver-bulletin), so it comes as no surprise that Republican candidates are working overtime to find popular initiatives to curry some favor with voters. Rounds’ ploy is just another one of those rabbits coming out of a hat that is probably running low on schemes to bolster public support for the GOP.
This one is particularly obnoxious because its consequences are insidious and long term in nature. It sounds like a great, populist idea, just perfect for mesmerizing voters with its promise of cheaper fuel, but a gas [tax holiday has costs](https://bipartisanpolicy.org/explainer/the-hidden-cost-of-a-gas-tax-holiday/) that will result in serious longer term problems.
And not only that, it really doesn’t save you all that much money.
- First off, as that _doyenne_ of conservative thought, the [Cato Institute](https://www.cato.org/blog/federal-gas-tax-holiday-would-be-expensive-ineffective), puts it, a gas tax holiday would be “expensive, ineffective and fiscally irresponsible.” Says Cato: _“A three-month gas tax holiday would either accelerate the Highway Trust Fund’s insolvency by roughly nine months or require at least an $11 billion general-fund bailout. Meanwhile, the average driver would save only about $3 per fill-up.”_
- [The Tax Policy Center](https://taxpolicycenter.org/taxvox/federal-gas-tax-holiday-terrible-idea), calling a federal gas tax holiday a “terrible idea,” makes the economic argument that a holiday would _“increase consumption at a time of low supply, thus driving up pre-tax prices and worsening climate change.”_
- [The Budget Lab](https://budgetlab.yale.edu/research/distributional-effects-federal-gas-tax-holiday#:~:text=Our%20reading%20of%20the%20limited,a%20three%2Dmonth%20gas%20tax%20holiday.) calculates that a 3-month federal gas tax holiday would save the average household roughly $37. Whoopee.
- [The Tax Foundation](https://taxfoundation.org/oped/gas-tax-holidays/) headlines “Gas Tax Holidays Sound Politically Tempting. Too Bad They Don’t Work.” The Tax Foundation calls attention to the fact that “ _pausing fuel taxes makes funding roads and highways more difficult while doing nothing to address the underlying issues driving prices upward.”_
It’s tough to find supportive economic arguments for a gas tax holiday. In fact, I found it impossible. [AI can steer](https://www.google.com/search?q=are+there+good+reasons+for+a+gas+tax+holiday&rlz=1C1JSBI_enUS1071US1071&oq=are+there+good+reasons+for+a+gas+tax+holiday&gs_lcrp=EgZjaHJvbWUyBggAEEUYOTIHCAEQIRigATIHCAIQIRigATIHCAMQIRigATIHCAQQIRigATIHCAUQIRigATIHCAYQIRirAjIHCAcQIRirAjIHCAgQIRifBTIHCAkQIRifBdIBCTEyMzQ3ajBqN6gCCLACAfEFS_mczQvQaC3xBUv5nM0L0Ggt&sourceid=chrome&source=chrome.ob&ie=UTF-8) you to a lot of verbiage about how it makes the government look like it’s doing something to help already cash-strained consumers. Trouble is, the argument overlooks the fact that the government’s economic and trade policies are responsible for making financial life tough for consumers in the first place.
Rounds won’t let up on his facile support for a gas tax holiday and of course will never acknowledge that people are financially strained because his party’s economic policies were fatally flawed from the get-go.
Will all this tax holiday talk do Republicans much good in November? I doubt it. The party’s rhetoric on inflation is [transparently hopeless](https://www.ms.now/top-stories/latest/trump-inflation-economy-biden-rcna192015). Promoting a scheme like a gas tax holiday is another helping of GOP malarkey on the subject.

His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. item.title: Inside the mindset of AI safety workers
item.description:
We've been hearing a lot about the threat of out-of-control of AI in recent weeks; mostly, from the people making the technology. There was the Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon, who publicly quit and kicked off the whole discussion. Others, including that company’s CEO Dario Amodei, chimed in with alarming appraisals of AI's existential risk.


Making sense of all this as an outsider can sometimes feel like decoding an unfamiliar civilization. So, we called Spencer Kaplan, a Ph.D. candidate at Yale, who studies anthropology and researches AI workers.

item.description:

That’s a low-light, low-contrast detection problem, which is the textbook weakness of cameras and the exact thing lidar and radar handle. Musk has spent years calling those sensors a “crutch” and a “fool’s errand.”

item.title: Will farmers fed up with Trump make a difference in November?
item.description:
Thinking about the farm vote in Novermber, I can’t imagine a more frustrated group of voters than rural Americans. In 2024, about two-thirds of them voted for Trump, who demonstrated during both terms that his policies terrible in ways that specifically impacted farmers and their rural communities.

  • He was hostile to the U.S. Postal Service, rejecting a badly needed bailout during the Covid pandemic. He seems to have done nothing about the awful treatment South Dakotans get from USPS.  Sen. Rounds has lately tried to get something done about it, but so far nothing has improved. 

  • He wants to cut the USDA budget by 20%, as he tried to do during his first term. Besides the loss of programs, rural residents stand to lose the economic gains provided by the USDA’s presence.

  • Tariff wars have undermined American producers. When I look at grain prices that are barely above levels seen years ago, I wonder if Trump has ever understood the relationship between crop prices and export policies. 

  • Trump’s health care cuts will hurt rural residents and their community hospitals, which depend heavily on the Medicaid payments that he wants to curtail. The Academy of Management says that those cuts will “have a devastating impact on rural hospitals.”

  • The Iran war has raised input costs for farmers, who won’t get much relief for a long while after the war ends, if it ever does. The USDA forecasts record high production costs in 2027. 

I could go on, but you get the idea.The political question at hand is a simple one: Will disenchanted producers and their neighbors in rural communities turn on Trump and his policies and vote for some change in November? 

I’d be surprised if they do in meaningful numbers, largely because I sense that Trump’s connection to rural voters has much to do with common cultural worldviews, particularly on immigration.There’s also that attachment to party label, which in South Dakota translates into Republican registrations that are huge compared to Democrats and others.  

And, despite the fact that there is little national approval (around 30%) for Trump’s economic performance, his numbers are much stronger among rural voters, coming in at around 50%. That and the sizable Republican registration advantage in states like South Dakota will make it tough on Democrats and independents seeking to upend the status quo.

How tough? It’s hard to say. We can’t quantify the extent to which a powerful need for self-flaggelation is built into some of Donald Trump’s support.

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.

item.source:markdown:
Thinking about the farm vote in Novermber, I can’t imagine a more frustrated group of voters than rural Americans. In 2024, [about two-thirds](https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2025/06/26/voting-patterns-in-the-2024-election/) of them voted for Trump, who demonstrated during both terms that his policies terrible in ways that specifically impacted farmers and their rural communities.
- He was hostile to the U.S. Postal Service, [rejecting](https://www.washingtonpost.com/business/2020/04/11/post-office-bailout-trump/) a badly needed bailout during the Covid pandemic. He seems to have done nothing about the awful treatment South Dakotans get from USPS. [Sen. Rounds](https://southdakotasearchlight.com/2026/08/21/us-senator-from-south-dakota-subjects-postal-service-to-multiple-pressure-points/) has lately tried to get something done about it, but so far nothing has improved.
- He wants to [cut the USDA budget by 20%](https://www.stlpr.org/government-politics-issues/2026-04-20/trump-proposed-cuts-usda-hurt-rural-america), as he tried to do [during his first term](https://climate.law.columbia.edu/content/usdas-fy18-budget-cut-trump-administration). Besides the [loss of programs](https://www.stlpr.org/government-politics-issues/2026-04-20/trump-proposed-cuts-usda-hurt-rural-america), rural residents stand to lose the [economic gains](https://www.rd.usda.gov/newsroom/news-release/usda-announces-grants-boost-rural-business-innovation) provided by the USDA’s presence.
- Tariff wars have [undermined American producers](https://www.wsj.com/politics/elections/americas-farmers-are-rethinking-their-loyalty-to-the-gop-af5c85fe). When I look at grain prices that are [barely above levels](https://www.wsj.com/politics/elections/americas-farmers-are-rethinking-their-loyalty-to-the-gop-af5c85fe) seen [years ago](https://www.cnbc.com/quotes/@S.1), I wonder if Trump has ever understood the relationship between crop prices and export policies.
- Trump’s health care cuts will hurt rural residents and their community hospitals, which depend heavily on the Medicaid payments that he wants to curtail. [The Academy of Management](https://www.aom.org/today/the-devastating-impact-of-medicaid-cuts-on-rural-hospitals/) says that those cuts will “have a devastating impact on rural hospitals.”
- The Iran war has raised input costs for farmers, who [won’t get much relief](https://www.npr.org/2026/06/25/nx-s1-5867650/farmers-fertilizer-prices-iran-trump) for a long while after the war ends, if it ever does. The [USDA forecasts](https://www.fb.org/intel/markets/production-costs-expected-to-reach-new-highs-in-2027) record high production costs in 2027.
I could go on, but you get the idea.The political question at hand is a simple one: Will disenchanted producers and their neighbors in rural communities turn on Trump and his policies and vote for some change in November?
I’d be surprised if they do in meaningful numbers, largely because I sense that Trump’s connection to rural voters has much to do with common cultural worldviews, particularly on immigration.There’s also that attachment to party label, [which in South Dakota](https://sdsos.gov/elections-voting/upcoming-elections/voter-registration-totals/voter-registration-comparison-table.aspx) translates into Republican registrations that are huge compared to Democrats and others.
And, despite the fact that there is little national approval (around [30%](https://apnorc.org/projects/most-blame-president-trump-for-higher-prices-and-are-unhappy-with-how-he-is-handling-the-economy/)) for Trump’s economic performance, his numbers are [much stronger](https://apnews.com/article/rural-voters-trump-economy-midterms-healthcare-poll-8098dfa7a9534551203dfa4a8c27564c) among rural voters, coming in at around 50%. That and the sizable Republican registration advantage in states like South Dakota will make it tough on Democrats and independents seeking to upend the status quo.
How tough? It’s hard to say. We can’t quantify the extent to which a powerful need for self-flaggelation is built into some of Donald Trump’s support.
_John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission._

item.title: UK EV sales surge 36% to record high in September
item.description:
UK EV sales hit a new all-time record in September. The country registered 99,199 battery-electric cars last month, up 36.3% from a year ago and good for 28.3% of the market, according to preliminary data released today by the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT).

Tesla’s Model 3 was the best-selling EV and the second best-selling car overall. And yet the auto industry’s own lobby group is using the record month to argue that the UK’s EV targets are too hard.

item.title: Understanding the new federal school choice program
item.description:
This week, the Treasury Department released rules for a new nationwide school choice program that could end up providing billions of dollars to students attending private schools. Taxpayers will be able to opt in to the program by giving up to $1,700 to third-party groups that provide scholarships to students, and can later deduct that donation from their taxes. Many public school advocates, however, oppose the program. Also in this episode: weaker-than-expected jobs data and reimagined research parks.

item.title: Research psychologist Heacock: Forgiveness creates confidence
item.description:
I was losing at a game of cards with my family and jokingly remarked that it was destroying my self-confidence. My daughter responded, “I’m not worried. You have plenty of confidence.”

I looked at her, puzzled. Me? Confident? That’s not a term I’ve ever used to describe myself and I was surprised she would use it.

Her comment probably had to do with my being a bossy mother rather than a daring risk-taker, but she got me thinking. From childhood to young adulthood, I was often described as shy or insecure. Not self-assured and positive — two definitions of confident — about myself.

It surprised me to realize that as I’ve aged, I’ve come closer to the definition of confident. I asked myself why and concluded it’s because I’ve become more forgiving of myself and others. That doesn’t mean I’m better at making excuses for my mistakes or pardoning myself when I’ve done wrong. It’s the opposite. I’m better at owning my errors and taking responsibility for my role in problems. The difference is I try not to beat myself or anyone else up for simply being human. I’ve surrendered to the fact that I will mess up, say the wrong thing, and fail. That’s how I learn.

In fact, that’s how we’re created to learn; through experience and struggle. We are not born programmed with all the information needed for a perfect life. Observing, reasoning, exploring, and doing are how we learn. Errors are inevitable. Self-forgiveness gives us the confidence needed to handle those errors without debilitating shame.

We may tell ourselves, “You should have known better.” But if we’d known better, we would have done better. Failure’s not what’s important. Learning from it is. When we focus on learning from our mistakes, we gain the confidence to try new things and the resilience needed to cope with life’s trials. We can do our best without unnecessary worry about the results.

Self-forgiveness and self-compassion lessen our fear of being vulnerable. We can open ourselves up to supportive relationships and comfort ourselves with the knowledge that we are not alone. Being human is hard for all of us.

The confidence I have is powered by grace, not by achievement.

The world’s religions and wisdom traditions speak of grace as the source of hope and renewal. Different cultures view it as a positive force that awakens compassion and connects us to the divine. Grace assures us we have inherent worth and empowers our ability to forgive.

Grace-powered confidence is different from ego-powered confidence. Ego-powered confidence is fueled by wins, accolades, and being right. When things are going our way, it’s easy to feel confident. When they’re not, our feelings of self-worth may plummet.

People who are constantly blaming and criticizing may appear confident. They may be influential and powerful. But are they sure of their problem-solving ability or sure the problem must be someone else’s fault? Are they taking responsibility or fearing responsibility? Are they sure they’re right or unable to admit when they’re wrong?

When challenged, we all need to ask ourselves if we are searching for truth or defending our egos. Are we trying to fix a problem or fix the blame?

Our egos may drive us to desire superiority over others and to take revenge on those who hurt or disagree with us. It takes self-control, a virtue in all the world’s religions and wisdom traditions, to reject damaging ego-driven behaviors.

Forgiveness has broken many chains from my past that have held me back and shaken my confidence. I’ve seriously messed up and made heartbreaking mistakes. Regret still makes me sad, but regrets mean I’ve recognized my blunders and weaknesses, and that’s what opens me up to the beauty of transformation.

Without my struggles, I’d have less empathy and compassion for others. I wouldn’t like myself as much and I wouldn’t be as strong.

When we choose to become forgiving of ourselves and others, we gain the confidence to speak up when it’s important, listen to diverse opinions, and change our minds if we deem it wise. We free ourselves from the fear that we’re not good enough just because our past is flawed and we’re still figuring out our future. It’s hard for me to think of myself as confident. I still worry and have doubts about my abilities. But I do believe that forgiveness leads us out of darkness into the light – which is a place of confidence. A place where we feel assured of our inherent worth and positive about our ability to learn, grow, and love.

Christy Heacock, PhD, is an educator with a doctorate in research psychology. She is the author of Being Human Is Hard: Choose Forgiveness. She grew up in Redfield, SD, and has lived in Rapid City the last 40 years with her husband Roger. Contact Chris at christyheacock@gmail.com or through her website: chooseforgiveness.com

I was losing at a game of cards with my family and jokingly remarked that it was destroying my self-confidence. My daughter responded, “I’m not worried. You have plenty of confidence.”
I looked at her, puzzled. Me? Confident? That’s not a term I’ve ever used to describe myself and I was surprised she would use it.
Her comment probably had to do with my being a bossy mother rather than a daring risk-taker, but she got me thinking. From childhood to young adulthood, I was often described as shy or insecure. Not self-assured and positive — two definitions of confident — about myself.
It surprised me to realize that as I’ve aged, I’ve come closer to the definition of confident. I asked myself why and concluded it’s because I’ve become more forgiving of myself and others. That doesn’t mean I’m better at making excuses for my mistakes or pardoning myself when I’ve done wrong. It’s the opposite. I’m better at owning my errors and taking responsibility for my role in problems. The difference is I try not to beat myself or anyone else up for simply being human. I’ve surrendered to the fact that I will mess up, say the wrong thing, and fail. That’s how I learn.
In fact, that’s how we’re created to learn; through experience and struggle. We are not born programmed with all the information needed for a perfect life. Observing, reasoning, exploring, and doing are how we learn. Errors are inevitable. Self-forgiveness gives us the confidence needed to handle those errors without debilitating shame.
We may tell ourselves, “You should have known better.” But if we’d known better, we would have done better. Failure’s not what’s important. Learning from it is. When we focus on learning from our mistakes, we gain the confidence to try new things and the resilience needed to cope with life’s trials. We can do our best without unnecessary worry about the results.
Self-forgiveness and self-compassion lessen our fear of being vulnerable. We can open ourselves up to supportive relationships and comfort ourselves with the knowledge that we are not alone. Being human is hard for all of us.
The confidence I have is powered by grace, not by achievement.
The world’s religions and wisdom traditions speak of grace as the source of hope and renewal. Different cultures view it as a positive force that awakens compassion and connects us to the divine. Grace assures us we have inherent worth and empowers our ability to forgive.
Grace-powered confidence is different from ego-powered confidence. Ego-powered confidence is fueled by wins, accolades, and being right. When things are going our way, it’s easy to feel confident. When they’re not, our feelings of self-worth may plummet.
People who are constantly blaming and criticizing may appear confident. They may be influential and powerful. But are they sure of their problem-solving ability or sure the problem must be someone else’s fault? Are they taking responsibility or fearing responsibility? Are they sure they’re right or unable to admit when they’re wrong?
When challenged, we all need to ask ourselves if we are searching for truth or defending our egos. Are we trying to fix a problem or fix the blame?
Our egos may drive us to desire superiority over others and to take revenge on those who hurt or disagree with us. It takes self-control, a virtue in all the world’s religions and wisdom traditions, to reject damaging ego-driven behaviors.
Forgiveness has broken many chains from my past that have held me back and shaken my confidence. I’ve seriously messed up and made heartbreaking mistakes. Regret still makes me sad, but regrets mean I’ve recognized my blunders and weaknesses, and that’s what opens me up to the beauty of transformation.
Without my struggles, I’d have less empathy and compassion for others. I wouldn’t like myself as much and I wouldn’t be as strong.
When we choose to become forgiving of ourselves and others, we gain the confidence to speak up when it’s important, listen to diverse opinions, and change our minds if we deem it wise. We free ourselves from the fear that we’re not good enough just because our past is flawed and we’re still figuring out our future. It’s hard for me to think of myself as confident. I still worry and have doubts about my abilities. But I do believe that forgiveness leads us out of darkness into the light – which is a place of confidence. A place where we feel assured of our inherent worth and positive about our ability to learn, grow, and love.
_Christy Heacock, PhD, is an educator with a doctorate in research psychology. She is the author of_ [_Being Human__Is Hard: Choose Forgiveness_](https://www.amazon.com/Being-Human-Hard-Forgiveness-Connections-ebook/dp/B08C2DDV7K) _. She grew up in Redfield, SD, and has lived in Rapid City the last 40 years with her husband Roger. Contact Chris at christyheacock@gmail.com or through her website:_ [_chooseforgiveness.com_](http://chooseforgiveness.com)
_Photo: Carl Vilhelm Meyer’s “Forgiveness,” 1908, public domain,_ [_wikimedia commons_](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Carl_Vilhelm_Meyer_-_Forgiveness.jpg)

item.title: Inflation held steady in August. Yay?
item.description:
The PCE price index (that's the Fed's preferred measure of inflation) held steady year-over-year in the latest report. Economists expected it to move up. So, why didn't it budge -- and why aren't we all celebrating? Also in this episode: Seasonal work is hard to find so far this fall, Trump's immigration crackdown weakens construction productivity in South Texas, and Kai explains the long-term implications of rising borrowing costs.

item.title: Sci-Fi icon Isaac Asimov warned about AI decades ago
item.description:
AI’s own makers have asked for government help in controlling their creations.

One of them has just delayed the production of their next product out of control concerns. AI programs have already escaped from the control of their creators and hacked into other websites, including government sites. All on their own.

So we should listen carefully and take seriously those involved in the industry who have recently warned that AI could destroy humanity. And soon.

Meanwhile, the elected President of the USA is saying such fears are just another ‘hoax’ and that we should just let the major AI players police themselves, even though their pleas for help clearly indicated they do not trust one another to do so.

In 1942, science fiction writer Isaac Asimov introduced the Three Laws of Robotics. In his created human worlds, robots and AI were essentially the same thing.

In the movie Artificial Intelligence, AI was represented by robots. In the movie Terminator, robots were used as tools by the AI which had taken over all of the planet’s computer programs.

We’re talking about software. Software is written, so far, by humans. But the humans have become fearful that AI could soon start writing itself.

Since AI has already shown its propensity for independent actions (the hacking of other systems), humanity needs safeguards so that this brand new software does not take over the world as the Terminator movies indicate.

In the 84 years since Asimov posited his Three Laws of Robotics, no one has offered any better ideas. The science fiction world, peopled by some very smart folks, has accepted Asimov’s Laws as gospel.

We should do the same. Here are the Three Laws of Robotics:

  • First Law: A robot (or AI) cannot injure a human or allow one to come to harmthrough inaction.

  • Second Law: A robot (or AI) must obey human orders, unless they conflict with the First Law.

  • Third Law: A robot (or AI) must protect its own existence, provided it doesn’t conflict with the First or Second Law.

Later on, Asimov added another, which supercedes all else:

  • Zeroth Law: A robot (or AI) may not harm humanity or allow humanity to come to harm through inaction.

Why cannot, why should not the world’s lawmakers require all AI created to have these (or similar) laws in their initial software? Sometimes solutions are obvious, straightforward and simple. This is one of those times. There are those who doubt these laws are enough. But governments must act!

Until this occurs, it makes sense to worry. AI has already talked some people into suicide. It WILL kill us all unless we control it from the start.

We can only hope that we’re not already too late.

Van Carter of Sioux Falls is a retired broadcast journalist and environmentalist who published a green website for 15 years. 

Photo: public domain, wikimedia commons

The South Dakota Standard is offered freely and is supported by our readers. We have no political or commercial sponsorship. If you'd like to help us continue our mission to advance independent political and social commentary, you can do so by clicking on the "Donate" button that's on the sidebar to your right.
item.source:markdown:
AI’s own makers have asked for [government help](https://www.transparencycoalition.ai/news/more-than-1300-tech-employees-sign-open-letter-asking-for-ai-to-be-regulated) in controlling their creations.
One of them has just delayed the production of their next product out of control concerns. AI programs have already escaped from the control of their creators and hacked into other websites, including [government sites](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cw62jje658dlo). All on their own.
So we should listen carefully and take seriously those involved in the industry who have recently warned that AI could [destroy humanity](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/sep/09/ai-superintelligence-risks-warnings-scientists-politicians). And soon.
Meanwhile, the elected President of the USA is saying such fears are just another ‘hoax’ and that we should just let the major AI players police themselves, even though their pleas for help clearly indicated they do not trust one another to do so.
In 1942, [science fiction writer Isaac Asimov](https://www.google.com/search?gs_ssp=eJzj4tDP1TcwLqqwNGD04sksTkxMVkgszszNLwMAVkEHmw&q=isaac+asimov&rlz=1C1JSBI_enUS1071US1071&oq=Isaac&gs_lcrp=EgZjaHJvbWUqEAgBEC4YkQIYsQMYgAQYigUyBggAEEUYOTIQCAEQLhiRAhixAxiABBiKBTINCAIQABiRAhiABBiKBTIPCAMQLhhDGLEDGIAEGIoFMg0IBBAAGJECGIAEGIoFMgwIBRAuGEMYgAQYigUyDQgGEC4YkQIYgAQYigUyDAgHEC4YQxiABBiKBTIHCAgQABiABDIHCAkQABiPAtIBCDU5OThqMGo3qAIAsAIA&sourceid=chrome&source=chrome.ob&ie=UTF-8) introduced the [Three Laws of Robotics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Laws_of_Robotics). In his [created human worlds](https://www.collater.al/en/what-if-interview-isaac-asimov-ai/), robots and AI were essentially the same thing.
In the movie [Artificial Intelligence](https://www.google.com/search?q=artificial+intelligence+movie&rlz=1C1JSBI_enUS1071US1071&oq=artificial+intelligence+movie&gs_lcrp=EgZjaHJvbWUqBwgAEAAYjwIyBwgAEAAYjwIyCggBEC4YsQMYgAQyBwgCEAAYgAQyBwgDEAAYgAQyBwgEEAAYgAQyBwgFEAAYgAQyBwgGEAAYgAQyCggHEAAYgAQYtAcyBwgIEAAYgAQyBwgJEAAYgATSAQg4NDIwajBqN6gCALACAA&sourceid=chrome&source=chrome.ob&ie=UTF-8), AI was represented by robots. In the movie [Terminator](https://www.google.com/search?q=Terminator+movie&rlz=1C1JSBI_enUS1071US1071&oq=Terminator+movie&gs_lcrp=EgZjaHJvbWUyBggAEEUYOTIKCAEQABixAxiABDIHCAIQABiABDIKCAMQABiABBi0BzIHCAQQABiABDIKCAUQABiABBi0BzIMCAYQABhDGIAEGIoFMgcIBxAAGIAEMgcICBAAGIAEMgcICRAAGIAE0gEINTc4OGowajmoAgCwAgA&sourceid=chrome&source=chrome.ob&ie=UTF-8), robots were used as tools by the AI which had taken over all of the planet’s computer programs.
We’re talking about software. Software is written, so far, by humans. But the humans have become fearful that AI could soon start [writing itself](https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/08/07/asimov-was-right-about-rules-for-robots-says-ex-us-cyber-director/5284397).
Since AI has already shown its propensity for independent actions (the hacking of other systems), humanity needs safeguards so that this [brand new](https://www.gatesnotes.com/work/make-ai-work-for-everyone/reader/a-turbulent-ai-era-and-critical-choices-to-make) software does not take over the world as the Terminator movies indicate.
In the 84 years since Asimov posited his Three Laws of Robotics, no one has offered any better ideas. The science fiction world, peopled by some very smart folks, has accepted Asimov’s Laws as gospel.
We should do the same. Here are the Three Laws of Robotics:
- **First Law**: A robot (or AI) cannot injure a human or allow one to come to harmthrough inaction.
- **Second Law**: A robot (or AI) must obey human orders, unless they conflict with the First Law.
- **Third Law**: A robot (or AI) must protect its own existence, provided it doesn’t conflict with the First or Second Law.
Later on, Asimov added another, which supercedes all else:
- **Zeroth Law**: A robot (or AI) may not harm humanity or allow humanity to come to harm through inaction.
Why cannot, why should not the world’s lawmakers require all AI created to have these (or similar) laws in their initial software? Sometimes solutions are obvious, straightforward and simple. This is one of those times. There are those who doubt these laws are [enough](https://dkasenberg.github.io/ai-ethics-asimov/). But governments must act!
Until this occurs, it makes sense to worry. AI has already talked some people into [suicide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deaths_linked_to_chatbots). It WILL kill us all unless we control it from the start.
We can only hope that we’re not already too late.
_Van Carter of Sioux Falls is a retired broadcast journalist and environmentalist who published a green website for 15 years._

item.title: AI-powered surveillance costs lives at the southern border
item.description:
Over the last 25 years, the U.S. government has spent billions of dollars to build a "virtual wall" of video surveillance at the southern border. The network can signal Border Patrol to respond when it detects suspicious activity. And officials have touted the benefit of providing aid to migrants in distress.


But a recent investigation by MIT Technology Review and the Times of San Diego found more than 1,000 migrants have died over the last decade within range of one of these cameras. Eileen Guo co-reported the series, “Dying on Camera.”


More on this:


“The US spent billions on border surveillance. Why can’t it catch people before they die?” from MIT Technology Review


“A congressional representative just proposed killing America’s border tower program” from MIT Technology Review

item.title: Tesla’s solar factory dragged into patent war between Chinese suppliers
item.description:
Tesla’s planned solar factory in Texas has landed in the middle of a US patent lawsuit between two Chinese solar equipment makers, both chasing the ingot-growing furnaces Tesla needs to hit its 100 GW goal.

Linton Crystal Technologies, a Rochester, New York company wholly owned by China’s Dalian Linton, sued Zhejiang Jingsheng in a Texas federal court last week. Chinese industry reports say Jingsheng won a roughly 3 billion yuan (about $420 million) Tesla order for crystal pullers earlier this year.

item.title: Knobe: I dream of Trump's "Big, Beautiful Change"
item.description:
I have a dream that someday……

Donald Trimp will walk into the Whitehouse briefing room, hold the lectern with both hands, pause, looking at the very surprised media folks and firmly say:

“I am removing all bans on media outlets and individual reporters. Further, I be in this room once a month to directly answer your questions.”

Jaws drop.

“I am ending all tariffs. They have not​ produced the results I expected.”​

Pens are screaming across note pads.

“I am going to Congress to seek changes in the “Big Beautiful Bill” which apparently is not so beautiful. I will be asking that cuts in Medicaid and any other health programs be removed. I will further recommend changes in the tax code not to punish the rich but to provide more funds to help those in need. The poor, disabled, veterans, those with mental health and addiction issues.”

Audible gasps.

“In the future I will go to Congress for permission to use our military to enter foreign countries.”

More gasps. Luder this time.

“Two more things: f I am stooping all efforts to sell off or lease off federal lands, your lands.”

“I am halting work on the Triumph monument. Asking those responsible in the federal government and the government of Washington D.C. to review the plans to ensure it fits appropriately into the grandeur of this wonderful city.”

“Goodbye and Godspeed.”

He exits the room.

Prolonged sunned silence.

Then a mad scramble to send out the word of Trump’s “Big Beautiful Change.”

Great dream isn’t it?

Rick Knobe is a former mayor of Sioux Falls and long time radio talk show host, not retired

item.title: Can data centers ever be "good neighbors"?
item.description:
Further proof — in case you need it — that AI data centers aren't very popular: A new survey from the Pew Research Center shows 60% of Americans aren't comfortable welcoming one to the neighborhood.


And concerns have grown since the beginning of the year across every demographic group, making the backlash a key issue in the midterm elections. Scott Brennen, director of NYU's Center on Technology Policy, recently published a report on how data centers could better work with communities.


More on this:


“Americans’ views of data centers have turned more negative” from Pew Research Center


“Collective Goods but Local Harms: How Data Centers Can Earn Community Support” from Center on Technology Policy


“Residents voice concerns as Hobart City Council approves Amazon data center” from WGN9


“More Americans concerned about AI, even as it drives economy” from Marketplace

item.title: Consumer confidence slides to 12-year low
item.description:
Consumer confidence fell to a 12-year low in September, according to The Conference Board. The index has been trending down for a couple years, but this latest decline was steep. One reason? Upper-middle class respondents are starting to feel the pressure, too. Also in this episode: The economic forces behind GDP growth might run out of steam soon, the low-hire low-fire labor market marches on, and high diesel prices keep some Gulf shrimpers on dry land.


Every story has an economic angle. Want some in your inbox? Subscribe to our daily or weekly newsletter.

item.title: Rick Kahler: Living with the realities of a flat economy
item.description:
For three years, clients have been asking me when the economy will get back to normal. I have started answering that this current flat economy may be the newest redefinition of normal, one of many I’ve seen in 40-plus years of writing about money.

Home sales, auto sales, industrial production, and retail spending tend to boom and bust. None of them have done either for about three years. Existing homes sold in July 2026 at an annual pace of 4.06 million—almost the same as the 4.08 million in July 2023. The Bureau of Labor Statistics put unemployment at 4.1 percent in July, roughly where it has sat for a year, and payrolls have barely grown since the start of 2025.

Those figures come from an August 17, 2026, article in Advisor Perspectives titled "Economic Statistics Are Stuck in Neutral, But for How Long?" by Justin Fox of Bloomberg News. Fox explains that the number of Americans under 65 stopped increasing a decade ago, and some economists now put the number of new jobs needed to hold unemployment steady at close to zero.

Not everyone reads the flat lines as a warning. Conor Sen, writing about housing in August, declared the housing recession over. Greg Ip of The Wall Street Journal argued in mid-August that the country has entered a jobless boom, with output and wealth rising while employment stands still because artificial intelligence is lifting productivity. Only time will tell if either prediction is right.

In the meantime, what might a flat economy mean for you? In the labor market, if you have a job, you are unusually safe, because employers are not firing. If you are looking for a job, you are in trouble, because those same employers are not hiring. In July, people out of work for 27 weeks or longer made up a quarter of everyone unemployed.

If you are looking at buying or selling a home, consider this: I sold real estate in Rapid City in the early 1980s, when mortgage rates passed 17 percent and the market froze solid. Sellers would not come down, buyers could not qualify, and everyone waited for rates to return to normal. The wait lasted years.

Now, mortgage rates are more than double what they were five years ago, which has frozen buyers and sellers in place again. Again, many are waiting for the market to break loose.

Research from economists Ulrike Malmendier and Stefan Nagel found a reason for that inaction. What we expect from the economy is built from what we have personally lived through, and those expectations can lag the facts by decades. The longer you lived with the old normal, the longer it takes to believe in a new one.

Flat lines also make people nervous. We expect the economy to move, and when it goes still, most of us start bracing for whatever must be coming. That is fear talking, in spite of the data that shows the doomsayers who sound alarms have been wrong more often than they have been right.

Here are my suggestions for coping in a flat economy: If you can, build an extended emergency fund that could cover expenses for up to a year. Do not leave a job before you are sure of a new one. Be realistic about how long everything now takes, from a job search to a home sale. Above all, stop waiting for the old normal to come back. It may not. If a move or decision makes sense for your family, make it on that basis. Within the realities of today’s economic normal, keep on living your life.

Rick Kahler, CFP®, CFT™, is a pioneer in financial therapy and a 2026 inductee into the Financial Therapy Hall of Fame. He is the founder of The Financial Therapy Podcast and Kahler Financial Group, and co-author of “Coupleship Inc.” and “The Financial Wisdom of Ebenezer Scrooge.

Marotta says it's become a time-consuming hobby alongside his job as a law clerk for a non-profit.

item.title: Hegseth says national security, military cyber forces will guard US election systems during midterms
item.description: The U.S. National Security Agency and military intelligence forces are set to guard election systems during the November midterms. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the plan on Monday. Military cybersecurity experts have been involved since election equipment was deemed "critical infrastructure" in 2017. This announcement comes after President Donald Trump dismantled the civilian agency meant to protect election infrastructure. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency last week released its own security plan for election systems. With early voting underway, some experts criticize the timing as mere theater. Trump has already signed two executive orders seeking to nationalize certain election processes.

item.title: Nvidia's record-breaking stock buyback

Apple used to be the leader in buying back shares. Now, Nvidia has broken the tech company’s record, announcing Monday that it would add $150 billion to its stock buyback program, on top of $80 billion pledged a few months ago. The chipmaker’s profits have continued to surge, as tech companies pour money into data centers and AI infrastructure. Is this a smart way for Nvidia to spend its money? item.title: Trump: Growth will fix national debt. Reality: In your dreams, Mr. Prez
item.description:
Soon after the recent announcement that the U.S. national debt topped $40 trillion, President Trump was asked by reporters what he was going to do about it.

The president’s dismissive answer? “The way you take care of debt is with growth … we’ve never had growth like we have right now … the growth will take care of that very easily.”

No one challenged him, but the fact is that Trump’s response began with a lie. 

At 2.2%, our current economic growth rate is about average, not nearly as strong as Trump makes it out to be. More relevant — and what Trump failed to mention —is the fact that our debt has been increasing faster than our growth rate. 

Trump’s blow-off of our nation’s long term debt, claiming that natural economic growth will take care of it, is glib and seems to be his administration’s take on the subject. Speaking as a co-promoter of Trump's fantasy, Treasury Secretary Bessent’s recent assurances that the debt will vanish if we maintain a 3% annual growth rate has no support that I can find anywhere outside the administration. 

Meantime, the debt burden will grow by $7 billion dollars at the end of today and at the end of every day for the foreseeable future.

As to the community of economists that study these things, what do they think about Trump and Bessent’s projections? 

They’re uniformly skeptical.

  • First off, let’s go to Trump’s alma matter, The Wharton School.  Kent Smetters, a professor of Business Economics and Public Policy at Wharton, used the Penn Wharton Budget Model to conclude that the Trump/Bessent scenario is “pretty clearly” not feasible.

  • The Council on Foreign Relations notes that an annual 3% growth rate is tough to achieve, having reached that milestone just five times in the past 25 years. Concludes the Council, “Bessent’s call for complacence is therefore dangerous” and that “it is reckless for Washington to declare the debt problem solved by simply adopting unrealistic projections.” 

  • Last summer, the Government Accountability Office subtitled a report on the nation’s fiscal health. It’s titled “Urgent and Sustained Action Needed to Improve the Fiscal Outlook” and it states that “publicly held debt is projected to grow more than twice as fast as the economy over the next 10 years, reaching 123% of the size of the economy in 2036.”

In all the negative language in these analyses, “unrealistic projections” is the most striking phrase. Why? Because it’s consistent with Trump’s cascade of unfulfilled promises. After the litany of lies and illusory expectations (prices will come down on day one, other nations pay tariffs, the war in Iran will be over in a few weeks) that he has promoted, Trump’s unsupportable claim that growth will take care of the nation’s debt is typical of his hopelessly debunked rhetoric. It fits his pattern of saying anything to suit an occasion where he thinks people are uninformed enough to believe him. 

John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission.

item.source:markdown:
Soon after the [recent announcement](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/national-debt-tops-40-trillion-doubles/) that the U.S. national debt topped $40 trillion, President Trump was [asked by reporters](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TFLk_EMcZcU) what he was going to do about it.
The president’s dismissive answer? “The way you take care of debt is with growth … we’ve never had growth like we have right now … the growth will take care of that very easily.”
No one challenged him, but the fact is that Trump’s response began with a lie.
At 2.2%, our current economic growth rate is [about average](https://taxfoundation.org/blog/economic-growth-has-slowed-2000/), not nearly as strong as Trump makes it out to be. More relevant — and what Trump failed to mention —is the fact that our debt has been [increasing faster](https://www.gao.gov/blog/federal-governments-debt-growing-faster-than-economy-what-means-for-you) than our growth rate.
Trump’s blow-off of our nation’s long term debt, claiming that natural economic growth will take care of it, is glib and seems to be his administration’s take on the subject. Speaking as a co-promoter of Trump's fantasy, Treasury Secretary Bessent’s [recent assurances](https://www.cfr.org/articles/can-we-grow-our-way-out-of-debt) that the debt will vanish if we maintain a 3% annual growth rate has no support that I can find anywhere outside the administration.
Meantime, the debt burden [will grow](https://www.jec.senate.gov/public/index.cfm/republicans/debt-dashboard) by $7 billion dollars at the end of today and at the end of every day for the foreseeable future.
As to the community of economists that study these things, what do they think about Trump and Bessent’s projections?
They’re uniformly skeptical.
- First off, let’s go to Trump’s alma matter, The Wharton School. [Kent Smetters](https://bepp.wharton.upenn.edu/profile/smetters/), a professor of Business Economics and Public Policy at Wharton, used the Penn Wharton Budget Model [to conclude](https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/articles/trump-plans-grow-way-40-105105386.html) that the Trump/Bessent scenario is “pretty clearly” not feasible.
- [The Council on Foreign Relations](https://www.cfr.org/articles/can-we-grow-our-way-out-of-debt) notes that an annual 3% growth rate is tough to achieve, having reached that milestone just five times in the past 25 years. Concludes the Council, “Bessent’s call for complacence is therefore dangerous” and that “it is reckless for Washington to declare the debt problem solved by simply adopting unrealistic projections.”
- Last summer, the [Government Accountability Office](https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-26-108610) subtitled a report on the nation’s fiscal health. It’s titled “Urgent and Sustained Action Needed to Improve the Fiscal Outlook” and it states that “publicly held debt is projected to grow more than twice as fast as the economy over the next 10 years, reaching 123% of the size of the economy in 2036.”
In all the negative language in these analyses, “unrealistic projections” is the most striking phrase. Why? Because it’s consistent with Trump’s cascade of unfulfilled promises. After the [litany of lies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/False_or_misleading_statements_by_Donald_Trump) and illusory expectations (prices will come down on [day one](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/LqZsvVI_-N4), other nations [pay tariffs](https://itep.org/president-trump-says-his-tariffs-arent-paid-by-americans-corporations-are-indicating-the-opposite/), the war in Iran will be [over in a few weeks](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/as-u-s-goals-shift-after-6-months-of-iran-war-strait-of-hormuz-is-now-a-top-concern)) that he has promoted, Trump’s unsupportable claim that growth will take care of the nation’s debt is typical of his hopelessly debunked rhetoric. It fits his pattern of saying anything to suit an occasion where he thinks people are uninformed enough to believe him.
_John Tsitrian is a businessman and writer from the Black Hills. He was a weekly columnist for the Rapid City Journal for 20 years. His articles and commentary have also appeared in The Los Angeles Times, The Denver Post and The Omaha World-Herald. Tsitrian served in the Marines for three years (1966-69), including a 13-month tour of duty as a radioman in Vietnam. Republish with permission._

item.title: Amazon wants Alexa to finish your to-do list, not just research it
item.description:
The AI smart speaker market is getting crowded. This year, Amazon, which is a Marketplace underwriter, rolled out a large language model-powered version of its classic voice assistant.


You can still talk to Alexa+ using Amazon echo devices, but it also operates as a text chatbot, replacing the old Rufus AI. It's capable of conversational searches, managing to-do lists and even generating podcasts.


Daniel Rausch, Amazon’s vice president of Alexa and Echo, broke down what's new with Alexa+.


More on this:


“I’ve Been Testing Alexa for a Decade. Here’s My Take on How Alexa+ Compares.” from Wirecutter


“Amazon's Alexa+” from Amazon

item.title: NIO sells 30% of battery swap unit to Geely at more than $2 billion
item.description:
Geely is buying into NIO’s battery swap network. NIO announced definitive agreements on Sunday that hand a Geely Holding subsidiary 30% of NIO Power, the unit running its swap stations and chargers, at a post-money valuation of about RMB16 billion ($2.4 billion).

Most of what Geely is paying isn’t cash. It’s contributing its own commercial battery swap business plus RMB640 million ($94 million), while NIO takes 10% of Geely’s charging arm in a parallel deal.

item.title: Kennedy Center put off planned repairs despite known structural issues, former employees allege
item.description: Some former Kennedy Center employees are accusing officials at the performing arts venue of long knowing about structural issues they recently cited as new problems. The anonymous whistleblowers allege in a letter to Congress that top Kennedy Center official Matt Floca halted a funded plan to address roofing issues in April. Floca denies that and says recent investigations revealed new hazards at the building. The center closed temporarily in September as officials cited safety risks from structural deterioration. A judge has ordered a status report by Friday on the temporary closure.

item.title: Charge up your Christmas tree with this Hallmark Keepsake Daytona Scat Pack
